title: Number of 1 Bits
statement: You get an unsigned 32-bit integer. Write it in binary and count how many of its digits are 1. This count is also called the Hamming weight or popcount.

example.caption: 11 is 1011 in binary. Three of its digits are 1.

idea.sentence: x AND (x - 1) wipes out the lowest 1 bit, so loop until x is 0 and count the loop turns.

jargon.plain: The number of 1 digits in the binary form of a number. Also called popcount.
The right-most 1 digit. Subtracting 1 turns it into 0 and turns every 0 to its right into 1.

watch.inputHint: One argument: a number from 0 to 4294967295. Keep it under 64 to see a 6-digit row.

vars.meaning: number of bits in the integer (32 here)
number of 1 bits, at most b

compare.unit: loop turns (rough: the second one only turns k times, often fewer than b)

rows.name: Test each bit
rows.note: Check n & 1, shift right, repeat for all 32 positions.

rows.name: Clear the lowest 1
rows.note: One turn per 1 bit. A number with two 1 bits takes two turns.

rows.name: Lookup table
rows.note: Precompute counts for each byte and add up four lookups. Fast but needs the table.

fast.takeaway: Brian Kernighan's trick does work only for the bits that are set. For 32 bits both are constant time, so it is the habit that matters.

stages.title: Unsigned copy
stages.note: Read n as an unsigned 32-bit value and start the count at 0.

stages.title: Clear the lowest 1
stages.note: x = x & (x - 1). The lowest 1 becomes 0 and nothing else changes.

stages.title: Count it
stages.note: One 1 bit was removed, so add one. When x reaches 0, return the count.

edges.title: Zero
edges.why: The loop never runs. No 1 bits.

edges.title: All 32 bits set
edges.why: The longest run: 32 turns. In JS this is 2^32 − 1, which must be read as unsigned.

edges.title: Only the top bit
edges.why: Bit 31 set. A signed reading is negative, so a loop that tests x > 0 would stop at once and answer 0.

edges.title: One bit missing
edges.why: Everything but bit 1 is set. Each turn removes the lowest 1, so 31 turns.

gotchas.text: JS bitwise operators work on signed 32-bit integers. For n >= 2^31 the value turns negative (4294967295 | 0 is -1). Use x >>> 0 to get the unsigned value back.
Test x !== 0, not x > 0. A number with bit 31 set looks negative after a bitwise operation, so x > 0 stops early and gives a count that is too small.
n >> 1 is an arithmetic shift: it keeps the sign bit, so a negative number never reaches 0 and the shift-and-test loop runs forever. Use >>> for a logical shift.
Take uint32, not int. int is 64-bit and signed, and a negative int shifted right keeps its sign. math/bits.OnesCount32 does this in one call, but writing it by hand is the lesson.

recap.key: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest 1 and the zeros under it, so AND with x removes exactly that 1. Count turns until x is 0.
recap.complexity: Time O(k) for k set bits (at most 32). Space O(1).
